ingredients.name: Large red onions
ingredients.notes: thinly sliced; red onions are traditional, yellow onions work but give a slightly different flavour

ingredients.name: Pandan leaf
ingredients.notes: small piece, tied in a knot

ingredients.name: Jaggery or sugar
ingredients.notes: jaggery gives a deeper, more complex sweetness; white sugar is a common modern substitute

ingredients.name: Tamarind paste or juice
ingredients.notes: thick, not watery; lime juice can substitute for a sharper sourness

ingredients.name: Maldive fish flakes (umbalakada)
ingredients.notes: optional; adds traditional umami depth; omit for a vegan version

steps.instruction: Slice the onions as thinly and evenly as possible -- thin slices caramelise more quickly and evenly than thick ones.

Heat the oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pan over medium heat. Add the mustard seeds and let them splutter. Add the curry leaves, pandan leaf, cinnamon, cardamom, and cloves, and stir for about 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the sliced onions and a pinch of salt. Stir well, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook covered for about 4-5 minutes until the onions begin to soften and release their water.

Uncover and continue cooking over medium-low heat, stirring occasionally, for 15-20 minutes until the onions turn a deep golden brown and become jammy and sweet. Do not rush this step by raising the heat -- slow caramelisation is what gives seeni sambol its signature flavour.
Add the chilli powder and stir through for about 1 minute.

Add the jaggery (or sugar) and tamarind paste. Mix well and cook for a further 4-5 minutes until the mixture darkens, smells deeply caramelised, and comes together into a thick, glossy, jammy consistency.
If using Maldive fish flakes, add them now and stir through for 1-2 more minutes.

Taste and adjust salt, sweetness, and chilli. The finished seeni sambol should be dark brown, jammy, and sweet-spicy-sour in balance. Remove the cinnamon stick, cardamom pods, cloves, and pandan before serving. Cool completely before bottling. Store refrigerated in a glass jar for up to 2 weeks, always using a dry spoon.

source_site: hungrylankan.com, cross-checked against islandsmile.org, 196flavors.com, brownceylonesefood.com, boyeatsworld.com.au, thephotowali.wordpress.com, topsrilankanrecipe.com, and diasporaco.com
collection_method: scraped, cross-checked across 8+ independent sources; very strong agreement on the slow-caramelisation technique and the sweet-spicy-sour-umami flavour profile
notes: Seeni means 'sweet' or 'sugar' in Sinhala, and the sweetness here comes from the slow caramelisation of the onions combined with jaggery, not from an artificial sweetness. Seeni sambol is an essential component of lamprais (sl_045), is widely used as a breakfast spread on bread and buns (seeni sambol bun is its own popular street food), and is one of the first dishes served to guests at New Year. Maldive fish flakes add the traditional umami depth; omitting them makes the dish vegan but changes the character slightly. Patience during the caramelising stage is non-negotiable -- sourcing agrees the onions must be cooked slowly for 15-20+ minutes to develop the correct deep brown, jammy texture. Store using a dry spoon to prevent spoilage; it keeps for up to 2 weeks refrigerated.
